extracted.intended_audience: general readers; literary scholars, writers, journalists interested in the Nobel Prize
extracted.subtask_description: Summarises the rules, eligibility, nomination and selection procedures, interpretive guidelines, and criticisms related to awarding the Nobel Prize in Literature. Useful for understanding how candidates are proposed, evaluated, and chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alfred Nobel's stated literary criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: "in the field of literature, produced the most outstanding work in an idealistic direction"; prize established to reward those who confer "the greatest benefit on mankind".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This wording from Nobel's will is the formal basis for the prize and has been subject to historical interpretation. The Academy has read 'idealistic' and 'greatest benefit on mankind' in varying ways (see 'Interpretations of Nobel's guidelines').

rubrics_metrics.name: Award is based on an author's body of work
rubrics_metrics.description: Although individual works are sometimes cited, the award is based on an author's body of work as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Academy generally considers lifetime achievement rather than a single publication; nevertheless, on some occasions a particular work has been singled out in the citation (examples: Knut Hamsun 1920, Thomas Mann 1929, Ernest Hemingway 1954).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationality-neutral eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The prize is open to authors from any country; Nobel's will rejects consideration of the candidate's nationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since 1986 the Academy has explicitly acknowledged the international aspect; in practice critics note patterns (e.g., European/Western concentration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may nominate
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominators allowed: members of the Swedish Academy, members of literature academies and societies, professors of literature and language, former Nobel literature laureates, and presidents of writers' organisations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-nomination is not permitted. Nominators must be eligible; nominations from ineligible persons can be declared invalid (examples cited in historical archive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination deadline and receipt
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals must be received by the Academy by 1 February each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thousands of requests are sent, and the number of returned proposals has grown historically (e.g., about 220 returned as of 2011). Late arrivals have on occasion been withdrawn or moved to a different year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination validity and administrative rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominations can be withdrawn, declared invalid, or unarchived for administrative reasons (late arrival, ineligible nominator, self-nomination under pseudonym, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples include nominations declared invalid because nominators were ineligible, nominations arriving too late, or self-nominations under pseudonyms; such nominations may be removed from archives or shifted to another year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of nominations
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominations are kept secret for at least 50 years before being publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public access to nomination records is delayed intentionally; as of 2025 only nominations up to a certain year are available in the Nomination Database. Leaks or rumours prior to release are therefore unofficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee shortlisting and timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Each year the Nobel Committee examines nominations, narrows to around 20 candidates by April, and approves a shortlist of about five names by May.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the shortlist is approved, the next four months are spent reading and reviewing the five candidates' works, leading to a vote in October.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortlist recurrence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: No one can get the prize without being on the shortlist at least twice; many authors reappear and are reviewed repeatedly over the years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This effectively favors candidates considered over multiple years and explains repeated nominations and reviews for many eventual laureates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation and reading practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Academicians read works in their original language; if a candidate's language is not mastered by any member, the Academy calls on translators and oath-sworn experts to provide samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is intended to allow direct assessment where possible; use of translators/sworn experts is an official accommodation for languages not represented among members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting and majority requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In October members of the Academy vote and the candidate who receives more than half of the votes is named the Nobel laureate in Literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strict majority is required; failure to reach it can lead to postponement or no award for that year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize postponement / no award conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: If no candidate receives the required majority of the votes, the prize may be postponed and announced the following year; controversies within the Academy can also delay awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: years with postponed awards (e.g., 1949) and the 2018 award which was announced in 2019 after Academy turmoil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swedish Academy composition and appointment rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Swedish Academy is composed of 18 members who historically were elected for life; rules were amended in 2018 to permit resignation and allow removal for inactivity over two years; Nobel Committee members are elected for three-year terms from Academy membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These governance rules affect continuity, conflicts of interest, and the makeup of decision-makers; changes in 2018 altered previous lifetime-only permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize sharing and award mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: The literature prize can be shared between two, but not three, laureates; prize money is split equally if shared. Laureates receive a gold medal, a unique diploma with a citation, and a sum of money; laureates are invited to give a Nobel lecture and attend the prize ceremony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared prizes have historically been rare and sometimes interpreted as compromises; the diploma normally includes a citation explaining the award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'idealistic direction' over time
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Idealistic direction' and 'greatest benefit on mankind' have been interpreted differently in different eras (conservative idealism, 'wide-hearted humanity', focus on literary pioneers, international scope, human-rights-oriented idealism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Academy's shifting interpretation explains variation in laureate choices across decades and is central to debates over what kinds of literature the prize should reward (e.g., moral idealism vs. literary innovation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Documented criticisms and perceived biases
rubrics_metrics.description: The award has been criticised for Eurocentrism, political bias, favouring European/Swedish authors, occasional awarding of Academy members, and excluding many worthy writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms include lists of notable non-winners, discussion of political dimensions (e.g., selections seen as sympathetic to particular political stances), and commentary on the Academy's practical ability to compare works across languages and traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional recognition of a specific work
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the prize is for a life’s work, on some occasions the Academy explicitly recognizes a single work in the citation (e.g., 'principally for his great novel, Buddenbrooks' for Thomas Mann).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such explicit recognition is exceptional but recorded in historical citations; it shows the Academy can and does sometimes anchor a lifetime award to a particular work of note.
